report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, which President Trump called “Liberation Day,” the U.S. announced two tiers of new tariffs: a 10% baseline tariff on most imported goods, effective April 5, and higher “reciprocal” tariffs for selected trading partners, scheduled to start April 9. The higher rates replaced the 10% baseline for those partners; they were not added on top of it. (whitehouse.gov)
| Trading partner | Rate announced April 2 |
|---|---:|
| Lesotho | 50% |
| Cambodia | 49% |
| Vietnam | 46% |
| China | 34% |
| Taiwan | 32% |
| India | 26% |
| South Korea | 25% |
| Japan | 24% |
| European Union | 20% |
These are selected rates from the executive order’s original schedule. Canada and Mexico were excluded from this tariff package and remained under separate tariff rules. Some products were also exempt, including pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, and steel and aluminum already subject to separate tariffs. (whitehouse.gov)
The announced rates changed quickly: China’s rate was raised before the original 34% took effect, and most other higher rates were paused starting April 10, leaving the 10% baseline in place for most trading partners. (usitc.gov)
